question_text: An internal note reads, “PC was broken, fixed it.” What is the FIRST important piece of information missing?
option_a: The technician who closed it
option_b: The reported symptom
option_c: The final ticket category
option_d: The user's satisfaction rating
explanation: The record should begin with what the user actually reported so another technician can understand the problem before reading the investigation and resolution.

question_text: Which sentence belongs in a USER-FACING resolution?
option_a: The ProfileImagePath value and .bak SID key were corrected.
option_b: The user loaded a temporary profile after Event ID 1511.
option_c: Your profile was repaired and your files open normally.
option_d: Tier 2 should review the User Profile Service event logs.
explanation: User-facing updates should explain the outcome in plain language. Registry details, event IDs, and escalation instructions belong in internal technical notes.

question_text: A complete handoff should prevent the next technician from needing to do which of the following?
option_a: Review the documented evidence
option_b: Confirm the affected asset
option_c: Read the ticket history
option_d: Repeat the same intake questions
explanation: A complete handoff preserves the symptom, evidence, work already performed, current state, and next step so the user does not have to repeat the story.

question_text: Which items belong in INTERNAL ticket notes? Select all that apply.
option_a: Exact command output proving the fix
option_b: A friendly closing greeting
option_c: Event ID and source
option_d: What was ruled out and how
explanation: Technical evidence, event details, and eliminated causes help other technicians. A friendly closing greeting belongs in user-facing communication.

question_text: A technician writes, “Ran some commands, seems fine now.” What should be added before closing the ticket to demonstrate that the original problem was actually resolved?
option_a: Evidence that the original symptom was retested successfully
option_b: The technician’s opinion that the system seems stable
option_c: A list of unrelated commands that were available to run
option_d: A guess at the root cause even if it was not confirmed
explanation: Before closure, the technician should retest the original symptom or use an equivalent verification method and record the result. “Seems fine” is not evidence.

question_text: Why do organizations care about complete ticket notes?
option_a: They replace endpoint monitoring alerts.
option_b: They support handoffs, auditability, and evidence of work performed.
option_c: They should expose all technical details to customers.
option_d: They are required for Windows licensing.
explanation: Good notes create an operational record for handoffs, audits, troubleshooting history, and—in some service organizations—billing or disputes.

question_text: A user reports, “The internet is broken again.” Which response best uses clarification to narrow the scope before troubleshooting?
option_a: Is this the same problem you had last month?
option_b: I’ll reset the network adapter first.
option_c: Can you walk me through what you were doing and exactly what happens when it fails?
option_d: Does the browser icon look normal?
explanation: Current 4.7 expects active listening and clarification. An open-ended question that asks the user to describe the activity and symptom narrows scope without assuming the cause or making a premature change.

question_text: Why should a ticket avoid saying that a user “obviously deleted” a file?
option_a: It makes the ticket difficult to close.
option_b: It prevents the file from being restored.
option_c: It means the user cannot be contacted.
option_d: It is unproven and unprofessional.
explanation: Tickets are business records. Record observable facts and evidence; do not assign blame without support.

question_text: A technician is creating a new support ticket. Which THREE items are core intake information?
option_a: Technician's preferred troubleshooting method
option_b: User/contact information
option_c: Affected device information
option_d: Clear description of the problem
explanation: Current A+ 4.1 explicitly includes user information, device information, and a description of the problem as core ticket information.

question_text: Which record is primarily used to track the hardware, software, and peripherals an organization owns or manages?
option_a: Inventory list
option_b: SLA
option_c: Incident report
option_d: Rollback plan
explanation: An inventory list tracks organizational assets. More mature environments may use a CMDB for additional configuration and relationship context.

question_text: A USB headset has failed. Which asset-record detail most directly tells the technician whether the vendor may replace it at no charge?
option_a: Current IP address
option_b: Warranty coverage/status
option_c: Ticket severity
option_d: Maintenance window
explanation: Warranty coverage/status tells the technician whether the device is still eligible for vendor repair or replacement under the warranty.

question_text: What document or procedure explains how to return a system to the previous known-good state if a change fails?
option_a: SLA
option_b: Incident report
option_c: Rollback plan
option_d: Onboarding checklist
explanation: A rollback (or backout) plan defines how to reverse a failed change and restore the previous working state.
source_name: ExamCompass Change Management Procedures Quiz + CompTIA 4.2

question_text: Which approach best reflects professional appearance in technical support?
option_a: Always wear formal business attire regardless of environment.
option_b: Dress exactly like the user you are helping.
option_c: Appearance never matters in support work.
option_d: Follow the organization's dress and workplace requirements.
explanation: Professional appearance depends on the organization's standards and the work environment, not a universal requirement for formal clothing.

question_text: What is the main purpose of an asset tag or asset ID?
option_a: Uniquely identify a device or asset and tie it to its record
option_b: Show the device's current network speed
option_c: Replace the manufacturer's serial number in every situation
option_d: Determine ticket severity
explanation: An organization uses an asset tag/ID as a unique internal identifier tied to inventory, assignment, warranty, and lifecycle records.

question_text: Which statement best describes a CMDB compared with a simple inventory list?
option_a: A CMDB is only a list of employee phone numbers.
option_b: A CMDB can record configuration items plus useful relationships and context.
option_c: A CMDB stores only closed tickets.
option_d: A CMDB is a replacement for all monitoring tools.
explanation: A CMDB can track configuration items and relationships/context that help support teams understand services and dependencies; inventory focuses more directly on what assets exist.

question_text: What does an SLA help a support technician understand?
option_a: The exact technical root cause of every incident
option_b: The user's Windows password policy
option_c: Expected service targets such as response or restoration commitments
option_d: The physical layout of a motherboard
explanation: An SLA defines agreed service expectations/targets. Technicians use these targets when prioritizing, communicating, and escalating work.

question_text: A company has an approved repeatable procedure for installing a custom application. What type of documentation should the technician look for first?
option_a: SLA
option_b: Incident report
option_c: Asset tag
option_d: SOP
explanation: A standard operating procedure (SOP) documents a repeatable approved process, such as installing custom software.

question_text: Which document is most useful for making sure the same required IT steps occur each time an employee joins or leaves the company?
option_a: Onboarding/offboarding checklist
option_b: Rollback plan
option_c: Network topology map
option_d: Event log
explanation: Onboarding/offboarding checklists make repeatable account, device, access, and recovery steps less likely to be missed.

question_text: A business-critical system requires an urgent production change that cannot wait for the normal schedule. Which change type best fits?
option_a: Normal change
option_b: Emergency change
option_c: Routine inventory update
option_d: Incident report
explanation: CompTIA's current change-management objective distinguishes standard, normal, and emergency changes. An urgent production change requiring an accelerated process fits an emergency change.

question_text: Before deploying a new application update to many production workstations, what is the safest preparation when a representative test environment is available?
option_a: Deploy to every workstation and monitor complaints
option_b: Disable backups to speed deployment
option_c: Test the change in a sandbox or controlled test environment
option_d: Wait until users discover compatibility problems
explanation: Testing in a sandbox or controlled environment helps identify failures before the change reaches production.

question_text: Which statement correctly distinguishes a change freeze from a maintenance window?
option_a: A change freeze is only for security changes; a maintenance window is only for hardware.
option_b: They mean exactly the same thing.
option_c: A maintenance window prevents all changes until further notice.
option_d: A change freeze restricts changes; a maintenance window is an approved period when changes can be performed.
explanation: A change freeze restricts or pauses changes during a sensitive period, while a maintenance window is a planned time for approved maintenance or changes.

question_text: Why should a technician or change owner perform risk analysis before a change?
option_a: To estimate possible impact and likelihood of failure so safeguards/approvals can match the risk
option_b: To guarantee the change cannot fail
option_c: To avoid writing a rollback plan
option_d: To make the change automatically become an emergency change
explanation: Risk analysis helps the organization understand possible impact and choose appropriate testing, approvals, timing, backups, and rollback planning.

question_text: A proposed normal change could affect a large production service. What should happen before implementation when the organization's process requires a change board?
option_a: Make the change first and document approval later
option_b: Obtain the required review/approval
option_c: Ask one affected user for permission
option_d: Skip approval if a rollback plan exists
explanation: High-impact changes should follow the organization's required approval process before implementation. A rollback plan does not replace authorization.

question_text: What is the main value of peer review in a change process?
option_a: It guarantees management approval.
option_b: It replaces testing and rollback planning.
option_c: Another qualified person can catch errors, missing steps, or risks before/after implementation as required.
option_d: It automatically lowers the change severity.
explanation: Peer review adds another qualified set of eyes and can catch mistakes or missing considerations. It does not replace testing, approval, or rollback planning.

question_text: Three tickets are waiting: (1) a warehouse scanner outage is forcing orders onto paper and has a 45-minute restoration target; (2) one designer's PDF export crashes but other work continues; (3) a new employee cannot see a shared calendar but can continue orientation. Which should normally be worked first?
option_a: The designer's PDF export issue
option_b: The calendar-access request
option_c: Whichever user complains the most
option_d: The warehouse scanner outage
explanation: The warehouse problem has the greatest immediate business impact and the shortest target. Priority should follow impact, urgency, and service rules—not volume of complaints.
source_name: Nexus Service Desk fixtures INC2402/INC2403/INC2405 + CompTIA 4.1

question_text: A ticket must be escalated to Tier 2. Which THREE items make the escalation most useful?
option_a: Current symptom and business impact
option_b: Evidence/actions already taken and their results
option_c: A statement blaming the user for causing the problem
option_d: What assistance, access, or decision is needed next
explanation: A strong escalation preserves context, evidence, current state, and the requested next action. Blame is not useful evidence.

question_text: A frustrated user says, “IT never fixes anything. I need this now.” What is the best response?
option_a: Acknowledge the impact, clarify the current blocker, state the next action, and give a realistic update time.
option_b: Tell the user to calm down before you continue.
option_c: Defend IT by explaining how many tickets the team handles.
option_d: Promise the issue will be fixed within 10 minutes.
explanation: Professional support stays calm, acknowledges impact, clarifies facts, avoids arguing, and sets realistic expectations rather than making promises the technician cannot control.
source_name: Nexus legacy — Talking to Humans + CompTIA 4.7

question_text: Which explanation is best for a nontechnical user after correcting a DNS setting?
option_a: The NIC had an invalid recursive resolver configuration causing FQDN resolution failure.
option_b: Your computer was asking the wrong service for internal site addresses; I corrected it and confirmed the site opens.
option_c: I flushed the resolver cache and modified adapter DNS parameters.
option_d: DNS was broken. It's fixed.
explanation: The first answer is accurate, plain language, and explains both the cause at a useful level and the verified outcome without unnecessary jargon.
source_name: Nexus legacy — Talking to Humans + CompTIA 4.7

question_text: While remotely supporting a user, you notice a folder labeled “Payroll - Confidential” that is unrelated to the ticket. What should you do?
option_a: Open it to verify the computer is functioning.
option_b: Copy the folder path into the ticket for completeness.
option_c: Avoid opening unrelated confidential material and continue only with the work needed for the ticket.
option_d: Ask a coworker to look at it with you.
explanation: Support staff should exercise discretion and minimize exposure to private/confidential materials that are unrelated to the support task.

explanation: CMDB stands for Configuration Management Database.

explanation: A good change request makes the purpose, scope, risk, testing, backup, rollback, timing/change type, responsibility/approval, implementation, and verification/end-user acceptance explicit.

question_text: A user gives a vague report: “The program randomly stops working sometimes.” What should the technician do FIRST to narrow the issue professionally?
option_a: Tell the user to reinstall the program and call back if it happens again.
option_b: Ask only whether the computer was restarted.
option_c: Suggest that the user is probably closing the program accidentally.
option_d: Ask the user to describe what they were doing, what appeared on screen, and when the problem last occurred.
explanation: Active listening and open-ended clarification help narrow scope before the technician assumes a cause or makes a change.

question_text: A repair is taking longer than the time originally estimated. What is the best customer-service action?
option_a: Proactively tell the user the current status, give a realistic revised timeline or next update time, and follow up as promised.
option_b: Wait until the repair is complete so the user receives only one message.
option_c: Promise that it will be fixed very soon even if the technician cannot control the delay.
option_d: Tell the user the vendor or another team is responsible for the delay.
explanation: Current 4.7 emphasizes setting expectations/timelines, communicating status, and following up. A proactive realistic update is better than silence, blame, or an unsupported promise.

question_text: You are going to be 15 minutes late for a scheduled remote-support session because an earlier incident ran long. What should you do?
option_a: Join late without mentioning it because the previous incident was more important.
option_b: Contact the customer as soon as possible, briefly explain the delay, and provide a realistic revised start time.
option_c: Ask a coworker to pretend to be you until you are available.
option_d: Close the appointment ticket and wait for the customer to reopen it.
explanation: Professionalism includes punctuality and contacting the customer when delayed. The technician should communicate the delay and reset expectations rather than disappearing or misrepresenting who is providing support.
